MASLD pathogenesis converges on insulin resistance, ectopic hepatic lipid accumulation, and chronic low-grade inflammation, which together drive lipotoxicity, hepatocyte injury, and progressive fibrogenesis toward compensated advanced chronic liver disease [@Chianetta2026Emerging; @Dinkov2026untitled]. Visceral adiposity and impaired insulin signaling promote unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic free fatty acid flux, while oxidative stress and gut microbiota alterations amplify necro-inflammatory activity within the liver [@Chianetta2026Emerging]. Within this framework, glucagon has emerged as an underappreciated second axis of dysregulation alongside insulin resistance. Type 2 diabetes has traditionally been framed as a disease of insulin insufficiency, but the development of a high-accuracy glucagon sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay has clarified that hyperglucagonemia independently contributes to hyperglycemia and hepatic steatosis [@Kitamura2026Role]. Notably, glucagon receptor antagonists lower glucose effectively without hypoglycemia risk but have failed to advance past early clinical development because they paradoxically cause weight gain and worsen hepatic steatosis, whereas glucagon receptor agonism—when paired with GLP-1 receptor activation—appears to counteract this liability by increasing lipolysis, energy expenditure, and hepatic fat oxidation [@Kitamura2026Role; @Kushner2026Cardiovascular]. This mechanistic reversal underlies the rationale for dual GCGR/GLP-1 receptor agonists such as survodutide and mazdutide, though their cardiac chronotropic and blood-pressure effects require dedicated cardiovascular safety evaluation, an issue being addressed prospectively in the SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT trial [@Kushner2026Cardiovascular].

The rationale for multi-receptor agonism extends beyond glucagon. Zhou and Dong propose a multi-layered conceptual framework in which GLP-1 receptor agonist efficacy in MASLD is governed not simply by pharmacological potency but by structural (hepatic and systemic signaling integrity), contextual (baseline metabolic perturbation), and temporal (durability of pharmacological input) constraints, explaining recurrent patterns of limited efficacy in advanced fibrosis, metabolically milder populations, and after treatment discontinuation [@Zhou2026From]. Multi-receptor agonists that co-activate the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR) and GCGR alongside GLP1R, such as tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1) and triple agonists including retatrutide and cotadutide, are proposed to partially overcome these constraints by broadening the regulatory inputs converging on hepatocyte metabolism [@Zhou2026From; @Khan2026Tirzepatide]. Tirzepatide additionally increases insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and shifts gut microbiota composition toward increased Bacteroidetes and decreased Firmicutes while enhancing intestinal barrier integrity, illustrating how receptor-level pharmacology intersects with a microbiota-metabolite layer of regulation [@Khan2026Tirzepatide]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomized trials (961 participants) evaluating dual and triple GLP-1-based polyagonists—tirzepatide, survodutide, pemvidutide, retatrutide, and cotadutide—found significantly greater MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening (RR 3.32, 95% CI 2.28–4.84) and fibrosis improvement without worsening of MASH (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15–1.94), alongside a mean liver fat reduction of −44.60 percentage points versus placebo, supporting the premise that expanding receptor engagement yields incremental hepatic benefit over GLP-1 monoagonism [@Santos2026Efficacy]. Zhou and Dong further argue that gut microbiota and their metabolites constitute a candidate systems-level regulatory layer integrating host metabolic, immune, and endocrine signaling; convergence across diverse interventions is more consistent at the level of microbiota-associated metabolic function than taxonomic composition, though causal significance remains unproven [@Zhou2026From]. This gut-pancreatic peptide axis extends further still, with glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, amylin, and peptide YY under active investigation as complementary signaling nodes in the evolving mono-to-multi-agonist therapeutic landscape [@Patil2026The].

Genetic variation in lipid handling further modifies treatment response and helps explain heterogeneity in liver fat reduction. The patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing 3 (PNPLA3) I148M variant is strongly associated with steatotic liver disease, and a post hoc analysis of the SURPASS-3 MRI substudy examined whether presence of the I148M allele (genotypes GG/CG) versus its absence (genotype CC) modified the liver fat content (LFC) response to 52 weeks of tirzepatide versus insulin degludec in insulin-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes and MASLD; tirzepatide produced significant LFC, weight, and HbA1c reductions across genotype strata, indicating that the drug's hepatic benefit is not abrogated by this common risk allele [@Cusi2026Liver]. Genetic modulation is not confined to PNPLA3: a propensity-matched genotyping study of GLP1R polymorphisms found that the rs761387 G allele independently predicted a blunted glycemic response to subcutaneous GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy (β = −0.277, p = 0.018), even as GLP-1RA outperformed SGLT2 inhibitors overall on HbA1c, BMI, and ALT reduction in patients with MASLD, underscoring that receptor-level pharmacogenomics, not just hepatic lipid genetics, shapes individual response [@Toffoli2026Comparative]. Choline metabolism represents an adjacent, less-studied pathway in hepatic triglyceride regulation: low choline intake is linked to obesity, MASLD, and type 2 diabetes, and circulating trimethylamine N-oxide is now understood as a marker of obesity- and diet-driven metabolic dysfunction rather than a direct consequence of dietary choline; whether GLP-1 receptor agonist-induced changes in intake and body composition alter choline requirements, and thereby hepatic triglyceride handling, remains an open question warranting investigation [@Paules2026Choline].

Translating these mechanisms into practice requires reliable identification of the treatment-relevant population, since fibrosis stage—not simple steatosis—drives liver-related morbidity and mortality and determines eligibility for resmetirom and semaglutide [@Li2026Liver; @Chan2026Pharmacological]. Inconsistent definitions of "at-risk MASH" have complicated this task. A prospective biopsy-and-MRE study of 413 patients proposed a simplified at-risk MASH definition (MASH with fibrosis stage ≥2) that captured a broader population (n=122) than the stricter NAFLD Activity Score-based definition (n=77), and found that MRE-derived liver stiffness (LS-MRE) alone had the highest diagnostic accuracy for at-risk MASH (AUC 0.91) and cirrhosis (AUC 0.93), outperforming FIB-4 and individual liver enzymes (p<0.01) [@Li2026Simplified]. Optimized LS-MRE cutoffs of 2.8–6.4 kPa, compared with AASLD-recommended cutoffs of 3.1–4.4 kPa, identified 25 additional biopsy-proven pharmacotherapy candidates—28% more eligible patients—while improving sensitivity from 50% to 80% with an acceptable trade-off in specificity (73% vs. 88%) [@Li2026Simplified]. This staging refinement has direct implications for trial design: agents with strong efficacy signals in non-cirrhotic MASH, such as fibroblast growth factor 21 analogues, have shown far less consistent benefit once fibrosis has progressed to compensated cirrhosis, reflecting disease complexity, patient heterogeneity, and the limitations of current histological endpoint frameworks in this population [@Zeng2026Drug]. Together, glucagon-inclusive multi-receptor pharmacology, microbiota-metabolite convergence, genetic modifiers of lipid and receptor response, and imaging-based fibrosis staging form the mechanistic scaffold against which the trial evidence reviewed in subsequent sections should be interpreted.
